questions.q: Gopal jogs 5 rounds of a circular park of radius 49 m in 11 minutes. Use pi = 22/7. Find the distance he runs in metres and his speed in metres per minute and in km per hour.
questions.a: One round is 2 x 22/7 x 49 = 308 m, so 5 rounds are 1540 m. Speed is 1540 / 11 = 140 m per minute, and 140 x 60 / 1000 = 8.4 km per hour.

questions.q: Anita does the home measurement for the C/D ratio. Her reel has diameter 2.8 cm and a thin thread wound tightly 20 times has length 176 cm. (a) Work out L / (20 D) and say what it estimates. (b) Why does she wind the thread 20 times and why must the thread be very thin? (c) Using her ratio, predict the circumference of a pan lid of diameter 14 cm. (d) Her ratio comes out slightly bigger than the true value of pi. Give one reason for this and say whether it shows that C/D is not the same for every circle.
questions.a: (a) 176 / (20 x 2.8) = 176 / 56 = 3.142857, the C/D ratio of the reel. (b) Twenty turns spread any small measuring error over many turns, and a thin thread does not add to the reel's diameter. (c) 14 x 3.142857 = 44 cm. (d) Small errors, for example a loose wrap or a thread that is not thin, can make the length slightly large; this does not mean that C/D varies, since the ratio is the same for all circles.

Part (b): turns spread the error and a thin thread does not change the diameter
Part (d): a measurement slip as the reason
Part (d): states that the ratio still does not depend on the circle

questions.a: (a) 3-14 suggests 3.14 and 22-7 suggests 22/7. (b) 3.14 differs from pi by about 0.00159 and 22/7 by about 0.00126, so 22/7 is closer.

questions.q: Show that pi cannot be exactly equal to Aryabhata's value 3.1416 (that is, 62832/20000), even though the value is correct to four decimal places.
questions.a: If pi = 62832/20000, then pi would be a ratio of two integers. But pi is irrational (Lambert, 1761) and cannot be written as a ratio of integers. Also, pi = 3.14159265... differs from 3.1416 in the sixth decimal, so 3.1416 is only an approximation, the 'asanna' value.

questions.q: Meera says: 'If I add the terms of Madhava's series one at a time and multiply the running total by 4, my estimates of pi alternately go above and below the true value.' Check her claim with the first four terms.

questions.q: Ravi adds the first five terms of Madhava's series, 1 - 1/3 + 1/5 - 1/7 + 1/9, and multiplies by 4. Find his estimate of pi and its error. Is it a better estimate than 22/7?

questions.a: (a) Errors: 22/7 about 0.00126; 3.1416 about 0.0000073; root 10 about 0.0207. (b) 3.1416, then 22/7, then root 10. (c) Brahmagupta chose root 10 for its elegance and the ease with which it could be handled in equations. (d) 14 x root 10 = 44.27 m and 14 x 22/7 = 44 m, a difference of about 0.27 m.
s: Part (c): elegance and ease of use in equations

questions.q: The chapter dates Archimedes to 250 BCE, Zu Chongzhi to 480 CE, Aryabhata to 499 CE and Brahmagupta to 628 CE. (a) How many years separate Archimedes from Zu Chongzhi? (b) The chapter says 355/113 stayed the most accurate value for over 800 years. Before what year, at the earliest, was it still the best? (c) How many years separate Aryabhata from Brahmagupta? (d) Aryabhata's word 'asanna' is said to suggest the ratio is not a simple fraction. Judge whether the chapter claims Aryabhata proved pi is irrational, and say who showed it and when.
questions.a: (a) 250 BCE to 480 CE is 250 + 480 = 730 years (there is no year 0). (b) 480 + 800 = 1280 CE, so it was the best until at least about 1280 CE. (c) 628 - 499 = 129 years. (d) No. The chapter says only that he 'regarded' or 'suggested' this; Lambert showed that pi is irrational in 1761.
s: Part (d): says the chapter only suggests his view and does not claim a proof

questions.q: A town council is fencing a circular pond of diameter 100 m using straight fencing panels of 2 m each. Each panel costs Rs 2,350. (d) What should the council buy and why? Give the extra cost over the cheapest plan.

(c) Isha's plan: 157 panels cover 314 m, leaving a gap of about 0.159 m (16 cm). (d) Buy 158 panels, which cover 316 m, as the rule is to round up. The extra cost is 1 x 2,350 = Rs 2,350 over Isha's 157.
s: Part (c): Isha's plan leaves a gap of about 0.159 m

(a) Is the total after 10 terms above or below pi, and by how much? (b) Is the total after 100 terms above or below pi, and by how much? (c) Does the total after 791 terms beat 22/7? questions.a: (a) Below pi, by 3.14159 - 3.0418 = about 0.0998. (b) Below pi, by about 0.0100. (c) Yes: its error is about 0.00126, just under 22/7's. (d) The data support the first half: 100 terms give an error 0.0100, about eight times that of 22/7, and 791 terms are needed. But the statement is too harsh: the series is the first exact formula for pi, so unlike a fraction it can be pushed to any accuracy, and the chapter says it gave Madhava 11 decimal places.
s: Part (d): weighs slow progress against its being an exact formula giving 11 places

Shows the angle would be about 430 degrees

questions.q: A sector of a circle has radius 21 cm and angle 40 degrees. Use pi = 22/7. Find the length of its arc and the perimeter of the sector.
questions.a: Circumference = 2 x 22/7 x 21 = 132 cm. Arc = 132 x 40/360 = 14.67 cm. Perimeter = 14.67 + 21 + 21 = 56.67 cm.

questions.q: On a track with a lane width of 1.22 m, the runners in lanes 1, 2 and 3 run at the same distance from the inner border of their lane. With pi = 3.1416, find the extra distance run on the two bends by lane 2 compared with lane 1, by lane 3 compared with lane 2, and by lane 3 compared with lane 1. What does this say about the stagger?
questions.a: Each lane's bend radius is 1.22 m bigger than the one inside it, and the two bends make a circle, so the extra run is 2 pi x 1.22 = 7.67 m for lane 2 over lane 1 and for lane 3 over lane 2, and 2 pi x 2.44 = 15.33 m for lane 3 over lane 1. The same stagger of 7.67 m is needed between every pair of adjacent lanes.
s: 7.67 m for lane 3 over lane 2 and 15.33 m for lane 3 over lane 1
Concludes the same stagger between adjacent lanes

questions.q: A school builds a small track with two straights of 60 m each and two semicircular bends. The inner semicircle has a radius of 32 m, each lane is 1.0 m wide, and a runner keeps 0.3 m from the inner border of her lane. Use pi = 3.1416. (a) Find the distance run in one lap by the runner in lane 1. (b) Find the distance run in one lap by the runner in lane 4. (c) How much stagger is needed between lane 1 and lane 4, and between adjacent lanes? (d) The coach wants to copy the 7.67 m stagger from a 400 m track whose lanes are 1.22 m wide. Judge whether it suits this track.
questions.a: (a) 120 + 2 x 3.1416 x 32.3 = 322.95 m. (b) Lane 4 is three lanes out: radius 35.3 m, so 120 + 2 x 3.1416 x 35.3 = 341.80 m. (c) 341.80 - 322.95 = 18.85 m between lanes 1 and 4, which is 2 pi x 3; adjacent lanes need 2 pi x 1 = 6.28 m. (d) No. The stagger depends on the lane width, 2 pi x width, not on the length of the track; with 1.0 m lanes, 7.67 m is 1.39 m too much for each lane.
s: Part (c): 18.85 m in all and 6.28 m for adjacent lanes
Part (d): says that the stagger is 2 pi times the lane width
Part (d): judges 7.67 m as too large by 1.39 m

questions.q: Two circles of radius 10.5 cm are drawn so that each passes through the centre of the other. Their centres are A and B and they cut at C and D. Use pi = 22/7. (a) Why is triangle ABC equilateral, and what is angle CAB? (b) What is the angle CAD, and what fraction of its own circle is the outer arc that goes round the far side from B? (c) Find the total length of the two outer arcs. (d) Compare it with the total circumference of two separate circles of this size and say what the difference represents.
questions.a: (a) AB = AC = BC = 10.5 cm (each is a radius), so the triangle is equilateral and angle CAB = 60 degrees. (b) Angle CAD = 120 degrees, so the arc inside the other circle is one third and the outer arc is two thirds of the circle. (c) 2 x (2/3) x 2 x 22/7 x 10.5 = 88 cm. (d) Two separate circles have 2 x 66 = 132 cm. The difference is 44 cm, the two arcs lying inside the other circle.
s: Part (a): three radii equal so equilateral and 60 degrees
Part (d): difference 44 cm as the hidden arcs

questions.q: A town park has a sector-shaped lawn of radius 21 m and central angle 120 degrees. Fencing costs Rs 150 per metre. Use pi = 22/7. The council has Rs 11,000 for fencing and wants a straight side of at least 30 m along which a stage can be built. It is also considering a semicircular lawn of radius 15 m whose diameter is the straight side. (a) Find the arc length of the sector lawn. (b) Find the length of fencing needed for the whole sector lawn. (c) Find the length and cost of fencing for the semicircular lawn. (d) Does either plan meet both the budget and the 30 m stage requirement? What should the council do?
questions.a: (a) Arc = 2 x 22/7 x 21 x 120/360 = 44 m. (b) Fencing = 44 + 21 + 21 = 86 m, costing Rs 12,900. (c) The semicircle has arc 22/7 x 15 = 47.14 m, plus the diameter 30 m, giving 77.14 m, costing Rs 11,571. (d) Neither: the sector has no straight side of 30 m (its sides are 21 m) and costs more than Rs 11,000, while the semicircle gives the 30 m side but costs Rs 571 more than the budget. The council should raise the budget by about Rs 571 for the semicircle or accept a shorter stage.
s: Part (d): neither meets both, with the shortfall Rs 571 and a reasoned way forward

questions.q: On a 400 m track the two straights are 84.39 m each and the inner bend is a semicircle of radius 36.5 m. Lanes are 1.22 m wide and each runner keeps 0.3 m from the inner border of her lane. Use pi = 3.1416. In a one-lap race all runners finish at the same line. (a) Find the distance run in one lap by the runner in lane 3. (b) By how much does it exceed the 400 m of lane 1? (c) The starting positions are marked with a tape that is read to the nearest 0.5 m. Which mark, 15.0 m or 15.5 m ahead of lane 1's start, is the better stagger for lane 3? (d) Explain your choice by comparing who is favoured with each mark.
questions.a: (a) The lane 3 radius is 36.5 + 2 x 1.22 + 0.3 = 39.24 m, so the lap is 168.78 + 2 x 3.1416 x 39.24 = 415.33 m. (b) 415.33 - 400 = 15.33 m. (c) The mark 15.5 m is the better stagger. (d) With 15.0 m the lane 3 runner runs 0.33 m more than lane 1 and is at a slight disadvantage; with 15.5 m she runs 0.17 m less and is favoured by that amount. 15.5 m is nearer the exact 15.33 m, so it is the fairer.
s: Part (d): compares 0.33 m disadvantage with 0.17 m advantage

questions.q: A parallelogram-shaped tile has a base of 18 cm and a slanted side of 10 cm. The perpendicular distance between the base and the opposite side is 8 cm. Its area is
questions.a: 144 cm squared

questions.q: In triangle ABC, D is the midpoint of BC and P is any point on the median AD. The area of triangle ABC is 84 cm squared. Which statement about triangle ABP is correct?
questions.a: Its area equals that of triangle ACP, but its value depends on where P is
o: Its area equals that of triangle ACP, but its value depends on where P is
Its area is always 42 cm squared, whichever point P is chosen
Its area is always 21 cm squared, whichever point P is chosen
Its area is half that of triangle ACP

questions.q: A field is a trapezium with parallel sides of 120 m and 80 m, which are 50 m apart. Its area is
questions.a: 5,000 square metres

questions.q: Rectangles with whole-number sides all have perimeter 40 cm. Which one has the greatest area?
questions.a: 10 cm by 10 cm

questions.q: A farmer replaces a rectangular plot of 4 m by 9 m by a square plot of the same area. The side of the square plot is
questions.a: 6 m

questions.q:
Read these statements about areas.
Statement 1: A parallelogram with sides 6 cm and 9 cm must have an area of 54 square cm, as a rectangle with those sides does.
Statement 2: A median divides a triangle into two triangles of equal area although, in general, they are not congruent.
Statement 3: Two rectangles with the same perimeter and the same area must be congruent.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A median of a triangle divides it into two triangles of equal area.
Reason (R): A parallelogram can be cut and rearranged into a rectangle of the same base and height.
questions.a: A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: A trapezium has parallel sides of 30 cm and 20 cm and an area of 400 square cm. Its height is ___ cm.
An isosceles trapezium has parallel sides of 32 cm and 14 cm, and each slanting side is 15 cm. (a) Find its height. (b) Find its area.
questions.a: (a) The ends stick out (32 - 14)/2 = 9 cm on each side, so the height is root(15 squared - 9 squared) = 12 cm. (b) Area = 1/2 x (32 + 14) x 12 = 276 square cm.
s: Part (a): 9 cm projection and height 12 cm

questions.q: True or False: When a median divides a triangle into two triangles, the two triangles are congruent. Give a reason.
questions.a: False. They have equal bases and the same height, so their areas are equal, but in general they are differently shaped (not congruent).
s: Says equal area comes from equal bases and common height, not from congruence

questions.q: Rectangles can be drawn with perimeter 40 cm and sides that need not be whole numbers. (a) Find the areas of the rectangles 15 by 5, 12 by 8 and 10 by 10. (b) Is there a rectangle of smallest area? Use 19.9 by 0.1 as a clue.
questions.a: (a) 75, 96 and 100 square cm. (b) No. The rectangle 19.9 by 0.1 has area 1.99 square cm and one can keep making a side smaller, so the area can be made as small as one likes but never reaches a smallest value.
s: Part (b): no smallest, since the area 1.99 can be reduced further

questions.q: In triangle ABC the area is 90 square cm and D is the midpoint of BC. P is a point on AD, and the area of triangle PBD is 12 square cm. (a) Find the area of triangle ABD. (b) Find the area of triangle ABP and the area of triangle ACP.
questions.a: (a) A median halves the area, so triangle ABD is 45 square cm. (b) Triangle ABP = 45 - 12 = 33 square cm, and triangle ACP is also 33 square cm, since P lies on the median.
s: Part (b): 33 square cm for both triangles

questions.q: P is any point inside square ABCD of side 12 cm. (a) What is the ratio of the total area of triangles PAB and PCD to the total area of triangles PBC and PDA? (b) Find each total.
questions.a: (a) The ratio is 1 : 1. (b) Each pair has heights that add up to 12 cm on bases of 12 cm, so each total is 1/2 x 12 x 12 = 72 square cm, whatever the position of P.
s: Part (b): 72 square cm for each total

questions.q: Sana says: 'My parallelogram has sides 8 cm and 5 cm, so its area is 8 x 5 = 40 square cm, as for a rectangle.' Test her claim.
questions.a: She is wrong. The area is base x perpendicular height, and the height is the perpendicular distance between the sides, which is less than the slanting side 5 cm unless the angle is a right angle. For example, a height of 3 cm gives 24 square cm and 4 cm gives 32 square cm. The sides alone do not fix the area.
s: Uses area = base x height with height below the slant side
Gives an example with a different area, such as 24 square cm

questions.q: Write a real situation whose area is worked out as 1/2 x (12 + 20) x 9. State the shape, what the numbers mean, the units and the answer.
questions.a: For example, a plot shaped like a trapezium whose parallel sides are 12 m and 20 m and which are 9 m apart: area = 1/2 x 32 x 9 = 144 square metres.
s: Names a trapezium with parallel sides 12 and 20
Says 9 is the distance between the parallel sides

questions.q: Show that no rectangle with perimeter 40 cm can have an area of 101 square cm.
questions.a: Length plus width is 20 cm. If one side is 10 + x the other is 10 - x, so the area is 100 - x squared, which is at most 100. The largest area is 100 square cm, for the 10 by 10 square, so 101 is impossible.
s: Writes the area as 100 minus a square
Concludes the area is at most 100, so 101 cannot occur

questions.q: Rahul says: 'A right-angled triangle and an obtuse triangle that each have a base of 14 cm and a height of 6 cm have the same area.' Test his claim.
questions.a: He is right. The area of a triangle is 1/2 x base x height whatever its shape, so each has area 1/2 x 14 x 6 = 42 square cm, even though the triangles are differently shaped.
s: Uses the 1/2 x base x height formula
Gets 42 square cm for each and notes the shapes differ

questions.q: A trapezium has parallel sides of 14 cm and 26 cm, which are 9 cm apart. (a) A diagonal cuts it into two triangles. Find the area of each, saying why the heights are equal. (b) Add them to get the area of the trapezium. (c) Two copies of the trapezium are joined to make a parallelogram. Find its base and area. (d) Show that the area of one trapezium from part (c) agrees with part (b).
questions.a: (a) The triangle on the side 14 has area 1/2 x 14 x 9 = 63 and the triangle on the side 26 has area 1/2 x 26 x 9 = 117; both heights are the distance between the parallel sides, 9 cm. (b) 63 + 117 = 180 square cm. (c) The parallelogram has base 14 + 26 = 40 cm and height 9 cm, so the area is 360 square cm. (d) One trapezium is half of it, 180 square cm, equal to 1/2 x (14 + 26) x 9.
s: Part (a): 63 and 117 with the common height 9 cm
Part (c): base 40 cm and area 360 square cm
Part (d): links to the formula 1/2 x (sum of parallel sides) x height

questions.q: Use Baudhayana's squaring of a rectangle ABCD with AD = a = 25 cm and AB = b = 9 cm. E is on AD with AE = b, F is the midpoint of ED, AFGH is a square and H lies on AB produced. An arc with centre H and radius HK = HG meets BC at K. (a) Find AF. (b) Find BH. (c) In the right triangle HKP, with KP = BH, find HP. (d) Show that the square on HP has the same area as the rectangle, and write the general identity this shows.
questions.a: (a) ED = 25 - 9 = 16, EF = 8, so AF = 9 + 8 = 17 cm, which is (a + b)/2. (b) BH = AH - AB = 17 - 9 = 8 cm, which is (a - b)/2. (c) HK = HG = 17, so HP squared = 17 squared - 8 squared = 289 - 64 = 225 and HP = 15 cm. (d) HP squared = 225 = 25 x 9, the area of the rectangle. In general ((a + b)/2) squared - ((a - b)/2) squared = ab.
s: Part (d): the identity with squares of (a + b)/2 and (a - b)/2

questions.q: Mr Naidu owns a triangular plot ABC. The side BC = 120 m lies along a road and the perpendicular distance of A from BC is 85 m. He divides the plot between his two sons by a fence AD to the midpoint D of BC. Measured lengths are AB = 92.3 m, AC = 119.5 m and AD = 88.3 m. Fencing costs Rs 90 per metre. (a) Find the area of the whole plot. (b) Find the area each son gets, and say why the two are equal although the triangles ABD and ACD are not congruent. (c) Find the length of fence needed all round each son's plot, including AD. (d) The younger son has the plot ABD. The elder, with ACD, says the split is unfair because his boundary is longer. Judge whether it is fair, using your answers and the cost of the extra boundary.
questions.a: (a) 1/2 x 120 x 85 = 5,100 square m. (b) Each gets 2,550 square m, since BD = DC and both triangles have the same height 85 m from A. (c) Plot ABD: 92.3 + 60 + 88.3 = 240.6 m. Plot ACD: 119.5 + 60 + 88.3 = 267.8 m. (d) The areas are equal, so the split is fair in land. The elder son's boundary is 27.2 m longer, which costs 27.2 x 90 = Rs 2,448 more, so he has a reasonable claim to some adjustment, for example the younger son paying part of that cost; the median fixes areas, not fence lengths.
s: Part (b): 2,550 square m each from equal bases and a common height
Part (d): fair in area, but extra boundary of 27.2 m costing Rs 2,448 supports a claim for adjustment

questions.q: A shop makes display frames from four equal rods of 3 m each, hinged at the corners, so the frame can be pushed from a square into a slanting rhombus. A banner is fixed inside the frame and needs a frame area of at least 8 square m. The perpendicular distance between two opposite rods of the frame is its height. (a) Find the perimeter of the frame and its area when the height is 3 m, 2.4 m and 1.5 m. (b) What does this show about finding the area of a parallelogram from its sides alone? (c) Find the least height at which the frame can hold the banner. (d) The owner wants the frame pushed to a height of 2.5 m so that it looks slanted. Advise him.
questions.a: (a) The perimeter is 12 m every time. The area is base x height: 3 x 3 = 9, 3 x 2.4 = 7.2 and 3 x 1.5 = 4.5 square m. (b) The same four sides give different areas, so the lengths of the sides alone cannot fix the area of a parallelogram. (c) 3 x h is at least 8, so h is at least 2.67 m. (d) A height of 2.5 m gives only 7.5 square m, less than 8, so the banner will not fit. He must keep the height at 2.67 m or more, so the frame can lean only slightly (the square gives the most area, 9 square m).
s: Part (a): perimeter 12 m and areas 9, 7.2 and 4.5 square m
Part (d): 2.5 m gives 7.5 square m, so advises height at least 2.67 m

questions.q: A triangular park has sides of 13 m, 14 m and 15 m. Using Heron's formula, its area is
questions.a: 84 square m

questions.q: Maya finds the area of a triangle with sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm by Heron's formula but, by mistake, uses s = 12 (the whole perimeter). Which statement is true?
questions.a: She gets about 77.8 square cm, far from the true area, which is 6 square cm with s = 6
o: She gets about 77.8 square cm, far from the true area, which is 6 square cm with s = 6
She still gets 6 square cm, because s only scales the answer
She gets 12 square cm, which is double the true area of 6 square cm
She gets 36 square cm, which is the area of a square of side 6 cm

questions.q: A field is an isosceles trapezium with parallel sides 32 m and 14 m and each slanting side 15 m. Isosceles trapezia are cyclic, so Brahmagupta's formula gives its area as
questions.a: 276 square m

questions.q: A cyclic 4-gon has sides 9 cm, 10 cm, 17 cm and 0 cm (the fourth side has shrunk to nothing). Brahmagupta's formula gives its area as
questions.a: 36 square cm

questions.q: A triangular signboard is equilateral with each side 12 cm. Using Heron's formula, its area, to two decimal places, is
questions.a: 62.35 square cm

questions.q:
Read these statements about Heron's and Brahmagupta's formulas.
Statement 1: In Heron's formula s stands for the perimeter of the triangle.
Statement 2: Putting d = 1 in Brahmagupta's formula gives Heron's formula.
Statement 3: A triangle can be seen as a cyclic 4-gon whose fourth side has length zero.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Heron's formula gives the area of a triangle from the lengths of its three sides alone.
Reason (R): Brahmagupta's formula gives the area of every 4-gon from the lengths of its four sides alone.
questions.a: A is true but R is false.
o: A is true but R is false.
A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: A triangle has sides 17 cm, 25 cm and 26 cm. By Heron's formula its area is ___ square cm.

Match each figure in Column A with its area in Column B.
Column A: 1. Triangle with sides 3, 4, 5; 2. Triangle with sides 5, 12, 13; 3. Triangle with sides 13, 14, 15; 4. Cyclic 4-gon with sides 3, 3, 3, 3.
Column B: (a) 84; (b) 30; (c) 9; (d) 6 (all in square units).
A triangle has two sides of 9 cm and 12 cm and a perimeter of 36 cm. (a) Find its third side. (b) Use Heron's formula to find its area.
questions.a: (a) The third side is 36 - 9 - 12 = 15 cm. (b) s = 18, so the area is root(18 x 9 x 6 x 3) = root 2916 = 54 square cm.

questions.q: True or False: Brahmagupta's formula can be used on a rectangle of sides 8 cm and 6 cm, and it gives an area of 48 square cm. Give a reason.
questions.a: True. Every rectangle is cyclic. With s = 14 the formula gives root(6 x 8 x 6 x 8) = 48, the same as length x width.
s: Gives s = 14 and the value 48 and says that a rectangle is cyclic

questions.q: The sides of a triangle are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4 and its perimeter is 45 cm. (a) Find the sides. (b) Use Heron's formula to find the area, correct to one decimal place.
questions.a: (a) The sides are 10 cm, 15 cm and 20 cm. (b) s = 22.5, and the area is root(22.5 x 12.5 x 7.5 x 2.5) = root 5273.44, which is about 72.6 square cm.

questions.q: (a) Write Brahmagupta's formula for a cyclic 4-gon with sides a, b, c, d, including the meaning of s. (b) What does it become when d = 0, and why can a triangle be treated as a cyclic 4-gon?
questions.a: (a) s = (a + b + c + d)/2 and area = root[(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)(s - d)]. (b) With d = 0, s = (a + b + c)/2 and the factor (s - d) = s, giving root[s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)], Heron's formula. Any triangle is cyclic, since a circle passes through any three points not on a line.
s: Part (a): s and the product of four factors under the root
Part (b): reduces to Heron's formula, with the reason a triangle is cyclic

questions.q: A triangle has sides 13 cm, 13 cm and 10 cm. (a) Find its area by Heron's formula. (b) Check it by half base times height, finding the height by the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem.
questions.a: (a) s = 18, so area = root(18 x 5 x 5 x 8) = root 3600 = 60 square cm. (b) The height on the base 10 is root(13 squared - 5 squared) = 12 cm, so the area is 1/2 x 10 x 12 = 60 square cm.
s: Part (b): height 12 cm and the same 60 square cm

questions.q: Dev says: 'A 4-gon with all four sides 5 cm always has an area of 25 square cm, as Brahmagupta's formula shows.' Test the claim.
questions.a: Partly right. If the 4-gon is cyclic, it is a square and Brahmagupta's formula gives root(5 x 5 x 5 x 5) = 25 square cm. But the formula needs a cyclic 4-gon. A rhombus of side 5 cm leaning over (height 4 cm) has area 5 x 4 = 20 square cm, so 'always 25' is wrong.
s: Shows 25 for the cyclic case, which is the square
Gives a leaning rhombus with a different area, such as 20 square cm

questions.q: Gita says: 'Heron's formula cannot be trusted for a right-angled triangle, because it does not use the right angle. For sides 7, 24 and 25 it will not agree with half the product of 7 and 24.' Test her claim.
questions.a: She is wrong. With s = 28, Heron's formula gives root(28 x 21 x 4 x 3) = root 7056 = 84 square cm, and half of 7 x 24 is 84 as well. Heron's formula works for every triangle, right-angled or not, and so the right angle is not needed.
s: Shows 1/2 x 7 x 24 = 84 and says the formula holds for every triangle

questions.q: Using Heron's formula, show that there cannot be a triangle with sides 4 cm, 5 cm and 10 cm.
questions.a: The semi-perimeter is s = 9.5. Then s - 10 = -0.5, which is negative, so s(s - 4)(s - 5)(s - 10) = 9.5 x 5.5 x 4.5 x (-0.5), about -117.6. The area would be the square root of a negative number, so no triangle exists.
s: Shows the factor s - 10 is negative so the product is negative
Concludes a square root of a negative number cannot be an area

questions.q: An isosceles triangle has a perimeter of 40 cm and equal sides of 15 cm each. Find its base and then its area, correct to two decimal places.
questions.a: The base is 40 - 15 - 15 = 10 cm. Then s = 20 and the area is root(20 x 5 x 5 x 10) = root 5000, about 70.71 square cm.
s: s = 20 and the product under the root is 5000

questions.q: A triangular plot has sides in the ratio 4 : 5 : 7 and a perimeter of 160 m. (a) Find the three sides. (b) Check that a triangle with these sides can exist. (c) Use Heron's formula to find its area, correct to one decimal place. (d) Land costs Rs 1,200 per square metre; find the cost of the plot to the nearest thousand rupees. (e) The seller says the area is 1,400 square metres, taking half of the product of the longest and shortest sides. Judge his claim.
questions.a: (a) 40 m, 50 m and 70 m. (b) 40 + 50 = 90 is greater than 70, and Heron's product has all factors positive (s = 80, so the factors are 40, 30 and 10). (c) Area = root(80 x 40 x 30 x 10) = root 960000, about 979.8 square m. (d) 979.8 x 1,200 is about Rs 11,75,800, that is Rs 11,76,000 to the nearest thousand. (e) Half of 40 x 70 is 1,400, but the sides 40 and 70 do not make a right angle (40 squared + 70 squared is not 50 squared), so the rule is wrong; he overstates the area by about 420 square m.
s: Part (e): rejects the seller's 1,400 square m with a reason and the gap

questions.q: Treat the triangle with sides 13, 14 and 15 as a 4-gon whose fourth side is 0. (a) Find s for the 4-gon. (b) Find the product (s - a)(s - b)(s - c)(s - d) in Brahmagupta's formula. (c) Find the product s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c) in Heron's formula. (d) Why is it correct to use Brahmagupta's formula here? (e) Is Heron's formula a special case of Brahmagupta's, or the other way round? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) s = (13 + 14 + 15 + 0)/2 = 21. (b) (21 - 13)(21 - 14)(21 - 15)(21 - 0) = 8 x 7 x 6 x 21 = 7,056. (c) 21 x 8 x 7 x 6 = 7,056, the same, and root 7056 = 84. (d) Any triangle is cyclic, so the 4-gon is cyclic. (e) Heron's formula is the special case (d = 0) of Brahmagupta's, which is the generalisation, since it covers all cyclic 4-gons.
s: Part (e): Heron is the special case and Brahmagupta the generalisation

questions.q: A cyclic plot ABCD has sides AB = 39 m, BC = 52 m, CD = 25 m and DA = 60 m. A seller prices it at Rs 5,000 per square metre and says that the area is the product of the averages of opposite sides, (39 + 25)/2 x (52 + 60)/2. A surveyor will measure the diagonal AC for a fee of Rs 30,000. (a) Find the semi-perimeter and the area by Brahmagupta's formula. (b) By how much does the seller's rule overstate the area, and by how much money? (c) The surveyor finds AC = 65 m. Show that angles B and D are right angles and use the two triangles to confirm the area. (d) Should the buyer pay the surveyor, and what price should he offer?
questions.a: (a) s = 88 m and the area is root(49 x 36 x 63 x 28) = 1,764 square m. (b) The seller's rule gives 32 x 56 = 1,792, an overstatement of 28 square m, which is Rs 1,40,000. (c) 39 squared + 52 squared = 65 squared and 25 squared + 60 squared = 65 squared, so by the converse of the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem, B and D are right angles; the areas are 1/2 x 39 x 52 + 1/2 x 25 x 60 = 1,014 + 750 = 1,764. (d) Yes. Paying Rs 30,000 can save Rs 1,40,000; the buyer should offer Rs 5,000 x 1,764 = Rs 88,20,000.
s: Part (a): s = 88 and area 1,764 square m
Part (b): 28 square m and Rs 1,40,000 overcharge
Part (c): right angles by the converse of the theorem and 1,014 + 750 = 1,764
Part (d): pays the surveyor because Rs 30,000 < Rs 1,40,000, and offers Rs 88,20,000

questions.q: A school plans two triangular shade-sails. Sail P has sides 13 m, 14 m and 15 m. Sail Q has sides 9 m, 10 m and 17 m. Cloth costs Rs 480 per square metre and an edge rope costs Rs 60 per metre of the perimeter. The school's budget is Rs 45,000. (a) Find the area of each sail by Heron's formula. (b) Find the total cost (cloth plus rope) of each sail. (c) Can the school buy both? (d) If it can buy only one, which gives more shade for the money? Decide with figures.
questions.a: (a) P: s = 21, area = root(21 x 8 x 7 x 6) = 84 square m. Q: s = 18, area = root(18 x 9 x 8 x 1) = 36 square m. (b) P: 84 x 480 = Rs 40,320 plus rope 42 x 60 = Rs 2,520, total Rs 42,840. Q: 36 x 480 = Rs 17,280 plus rope 36 x 60 = Rs 2,160, total Rs 19,440. (c) Together they cost Rs 62,280, more than Rs 45,000, so no. (d) P gives 84 / 42,840 = 0.00196 square m per rupee and Q gives 36 / 19,440 = 0.00185, so P gives more shade for each rupee and fits the budget. Choose P.
s: Part (c): total Rs 62,280 exceeds the budget
Part (d): P gives more shade per rupee and is within the budget

The circumference of a circle is 88 cm. Use pi = 22/7. (a) Find its radius. (b) Find the area of a quadrant (quarter circle) of this circle.
questions.a: (a) 2 x 22/7 x r = 88, so r = 14 cm. (b) The circle has area 22/7 x 14 x 14 = 616 square cm, so the quadrant has 616 / 4 = 154 square cm.

questions.q: True or False: The area of a regular polygon equals half its perimeter times the radius of the circle that passes through all its vertices. Give a reason or correction.
questions.a: False. It is half the perimeter times the radius of the circle that fits tightly inside the polygon, touching its sides. For a square of side 10 this radius is 5 and the area is 1/2 x 40 x 5 = 100.
s: Corrects it to the inscribed (tight-fitting) circle radius

questions.q: For a shape of perimeter P and area A the ratio P squared : A depends only on the shape. (a) Find P squared / A for a square (side 6), for an equilateral triangle (side 4, area 6.93 square units) and for a circle (use pi = 3.14). (b) Of these three shapes, which has the smallest ratio and what does that say about the area enclosed for a given perimeter?
questions.a: (a) Square: 24 squared / 36 = 16. Triangle: 12 squared / 6.93 = 20.78. Circle: C squared / A = (2 pi r) squared / (pi r squared) = 4 pi = 12.56. (b) The circle has the smallest ratio, so among these three shapes it encloses the most area for the same perimeter.
s: Part (b): the circle, with the area-for-perimeter reading

A circular floor has a diameter of 9 m. (a) Find its area by the Egyptian rule (8/9 of the diameter) squared. (b) Find its area with pi = 22/7 and say by what fraction of the true area the Egyptian rule is out.
questions.a: (a) (8/9 x 9) squared = 64 square m. (b) True area = 22/7 x 4.5 x 4.5 = 63.64 square m; the difference is 0.36 square m, about 0.6 percent of the true area.

questions.q: Lata says: 'The minor segment cut off by a chord that makes 90 degrees at the centre has the same area as the sector with the same 90 degrees.' Test her claim with a circle of radius 10 cm and pi = 3.14.
questions.a: She is wrong. The sector has area 3.14 x 100 / 4 = 78.5 square cm. The segment is the sector minus the triangle formed by the two radii and the chord, which is 1/2 x 10 x 10 = 50 square cm, so the segment is 28.5 square cm. The segment is smaller.
s: Segment is the sector minus the 50 square cm triangle, giving 28.5

questions.q: Imran says: 'A semicircular plate of diameter 14 cm has area 1/2 x pi x r squared = 77 square cm and perimeter pi x r = 22 cm.' Use pi = 22/7 and test the claim.
questions.a: Partly right. The area is 1/2 x 22/7 x 49 = 77 square cm, which is correct. But the perimeter of the plate includes the straight edge as well as the curved edge: 22 + 14 = 36 cm, so 22 cm is only the length of the curved part.
s: Corrects the perimeter to 36 cm by adding the diameter

questions.q: Show that a sector of a circle of radius 7 cm cannot have an area of 200 square cm. Use pi = 22/7.
questions.a: The whole circle has area 22/7 x 49 = 154 square cm. A sector is only a part of the circle, so its area cannot be more than 154 square cm; 200 is more than the full circle.
s: Finds the whole circle's area 154 square cm
States a sector is a part of the circle, so it cannot exceed that

questions.q: Write a situation of your own in which the value 22/7 x 14 x 14 x (120/360) would have to be worked out. Say what the numbers represent and evaluate it.
questions.a: For example, a sprinkler on a pivot that reaches 14 m and turns through 120 degrees waters a sector of area 22/7 x 14 x 14 x 1/3 = 205.33 square m.
s: Names a sector with radius 14 and angle 120 degrees
Evaluates to about 205.33 with square units

questions.q: Take a circle of radius 21 cm with pi = 22/7, cut into thin slices and rearranged as in Nilakantha's method. (a) Find the base and the height of the parallelogram-like figure. (b) Find its area. (c) Show that Archimedes' triangle with perpendicular sides r and the circumference gives the same area. (d) The Babylonian rule A = C squared / 12 gives what area and how far is it out? (e) The Egyptian rule (8/9 of the diameter) squared gives what area, and which old rule is closer?
questions.a: (a) The circumference is 132 cm, so the base is 66 cm and the height is 21 cm. (b) 66 x 21 = 1,386 square cm. (c) 1/2 x 21 x 132 = 1,386 square cm. (d) 132 squared / 12 = 1,452 square cm, which is 66 more. (e) (8 x 42 / 9) squared = 1,393.8 square cm, which is 7.8 more, so the Egyptian rule is much closer.
s: Part (a): base 66 cm and height 21 cm
Part (e): 1,393.8 square cm, closer, out by 7.8

questions.q: A chord of a circle of radius 12 cm subtends an angle of 60 degrees at the centre. Use pi = 3.14 and root 3 = 1.73. (a) Find the area of the minor sector. (b) Explain why the triangle formed by the radii and chord is equilateral and find its area, which is root 3 / 4 times the side squared. (c) Find the area of the minor segment. (d) Find the area of the major segment. (e) Check that the two segments add to the area of the circle.
questions.a: (a) 3.14 x 144 x 60/360 = 75.36 square cm. (b) The two radii are equal and the angle between them is 60 degrees, so the other two angles add to 120 degrees and are equal, so each is 60 degrees. Area = 1.73/4 x 144 = 62.28 square cm. (c) 75.36 - 62.28 = 13.08 square cm. (d) 3.14 x 144 - 13.08 = 452.16 - 13.08 = 439.08 square cm. (e) 13.08 + 439.08 = 452.16, the area of the circle.
s: Part (b): the equilateral argument and 62.28 square cm

questions.q: A circular park has a radius of 35 m. The council divides it into sectors from the centre: a rose bed of 72 degrees, a fountain area of 90 degrees and the remaining lawn. Lawn seed and laying cost Rs 25 per square metre, and the lawn budget is Rs 50,000. Use pi = 22/7. (a) Find the area of the park and the areas of the rose bed and the fountain sector. (b) Find the lawn area and its cost. (c) By how much does the plan overspend? (d) The rose bed must stay at 72 degrees. What is the least whole number of degrees for the fountain sector that brings the lawn cost within the budget, and what is the fountain's new area?
questions.a: (a) The park is 22/7 x 35 x 35 = 3,850 square m; the rose bed is 3,850 x 72/360 = 770 and the fountain sector is 3,850 x 90/360 = 962.5 square m. (b) The lawn is 198 degrees, so 3,850 x 198/360 = 2,117.5 square m, costing Rs 52,937.50. (c) The overspend is Rs 2,937.50. (d) The lawn must be at most 2,000 square m, so at most 2,000/3,850 x 360 = 187.01 degrees; the fountain must be at least 360 - 72 - 187.01 = 100.99, so 101 degrees, with area 3,850 x 101/360 = 1,080.1 square m.
s: Part (d): 101 degrees and about 1,080 square m

questions.q: A pizza shop sells a large pizza of diameter 35 cm for Rs 420, cut into 8 equal slices, and a medium pizza of diameter 28 cm for Rs 280, cut into 6 equal slices. Each guest in a birthday party must get one whole slice of at least 100 square cm. Use pi = 22/7. (a) Find the area of each pizza. (b) Find the area of one slice of each pizza. (c) Find the cost for each 100 square cm of pizza. (d) For a party of 6 guests and for a party of 8 guests, say which choice is the cheapest that still gives every guest a slice of at least 100 square cm, with the cost.
questions.a: (a) Large: 22/7 x 17.5 x 17.5 = 962.5 square cm. Medium: 22/7 x 14 x 14 = 616 square cm. (b) Large slice 962.5 / 8 = 120.3 square cm. Medium slice 616 / 6 = 102.7 square cm. Both are at least 100. (c) Large 420 / 962.5 x 100 = Rs 43.64; medium 280 / 616 x 100 = Rs 45.45. (d) For 6 guests one medium pizza (6 slices) costs Rs 280, cheaper than the large at Rs 420. For 8 guests one large pizza (8 slices) costs Rs 420, cheaper than two mediums at Rs 560. Large is better value per area, but the medium wins when only 6 slices are needed.
s: Part (b): 120.3 and 102.7 square cm, both above 100
Part (c): Rs 43.64 and Rs 45.45 per 100 square cm
Part (d): medium for 6 guests at Rs 280 and large for 8 guests at Rs 420
